problems.description: Ripped out the seed's SQLite layer (ACID, transactional, multi-connection safe) in favor of a flat JSON file; the threading.Lock only guards single-process read-modify-write, so a multi-process/multi-worker deployment risks lost updates and file corruption.
_write() opens the store with 'w' + json.dump directly; an interruption mid-write corrupts the entire file. Write-to-temp with an atomic os.replace() would be more durable.
Every request does a full O(n) file read and linear scan (get_tasks/get_task); acceptable at todo-app scale but a step back from SQLite's indexed queries.

Mechanical scan reports a 0.70 convention score with 16 violations, but all listed violations are in pre-existing untouched files (celery_config.py, conftest.py, email_tasks.py, repositories.py) — none are introduced by this commit's new code.
The fixture monkeypatches the module-global DATA_FILE; safe here but the suite would collide if ever run under pytest-xdist or parallel workers.

strengths: Comprehensive test suite (11 tests) covering create, list ordering, get, update (full and partial), 404s, blank-title validation, and flat-file persistence — the seed had none.
Preserved the seed's public function signatures and route/error-handling seams (dict | None -> 404 pattern intact), honoring the designed 'good seams' baseline.
Thread-safety lock guards the read-modify-write path, and title validation was tightened with an isinstance check.
Module docstring kept in sync with the new flat-file design; DATABASE/data-file name is env-configurable like before.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested rewrite that preserves the API seams and adds real test coverage, but trades SQLite's transactional guarantees for a single-process lock-guarded flat file — a storage regression offset by the new suite.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-for-local-development-only' when SECRET_KEY env is unset, making JWT signing keys predictable in any deployment that forgets the env var.
SonarQube delta shows cognitive complexity +35 and +3 smells; the _migrate() backfill and auth_required() wrapper add non-trivial branch density to a single-file app.
int(payload.get("sub")) in auth_required can raise ValueError (500) on a validly-signed token whose sub is non-numeric; should be guarded like the other invalid-token paths.
Diff adds +28 functions and new /auth/register + /auth/login endpoints but +0 files touched — no tests added for the new auth/owner-scoping behavior.

Measured convention score (0.70, 16 violations) is dominated by violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, conftest.py, email_tasks.py, repositories.py); the app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' violation matches no class in this diff — the score appears to reflect pre-existing debt, not this commit.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+; utcnow() is used in both token_for() and create_task().

strengths: Owner-scoping is threaded consistently through get_tasks/get_task/update_task/create_task, so every access path enforces the same authorization boundary.
_migrate() upgrades legacy flat-file stores in place without destroying data, backfilling ownerless tasks to a dedicated 'legacy' user.
Adheres to the codebase's established conventions: snake_case, type hints on public signatures, section-comment banners matching existing style, flat-file storage + threading.Lock pattern preserved.
Auth uses idiomatic primitives (functools.wraps decorator, werkzeug password hashing, g.current_user) and returns consistent 400/401/409 status codes.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped feature addition that extends the existing flat-file architecture with owner-scoped JWT auth and a careful in-place migration, though it carries modest debt from a hardcoded dev SECRET_KEY fallback, a +35 complexity bump, and no new tests.

problems.description: Notification business logic (status-transition detection + email dispatch) lives in the Flask route handler `edit_task`; the domain rule 'notify on transition to completed' belongs in the service/model layer so it is testable and reusable independent of HTTP.

send_notification_email.delay() is a synchronous failure point in the request path — if the Celery broker is down, a completed task PUT raises and returns 500 even though the update already succeeded. Fire-and-forget with a try/except (or pre-task queue check) is more robust.
Email-defaulting logic `f"{username}@example.com"` is duplicated in edit_task, create_user, and the legacy migration; create_user already defaults the field so the route-level fallback is redundant.
Request `email` is not validated as a str (unlike username/password), so a non-string email flows into create_user and the store.

Notification trigger is only tested via monkeypatched `delay`; there is no test that the Celery task is registered/executable against the configured app, so a wiring break (e.g. wrong `include` or task name) would go undetected.

strengths: Notification is only fired on a genuine status transition (current != completed check), preserving idempotency for repeated completed PUTs
Defensive 404 added to edit_task before mutation, consistent with existing validation style
Fixtures cleanly extracted from test_app.py into conftest.py, and notification tests are isolated from the broker via monkeypatch
Coherent integration step: email_tasks.py, celery_config.py, and app.py wiring follow a clean single-responsibility split with type hints
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested Celery integration step (fixtures extracted, defensive 404, transition-aware notification) that is overall an improvement, though the notification rule is embedded in the route handler, broker failure can 500 an already-successful update, and the measured 0.70 convention score appears overstated — the 16 flagged violations (e.g. PascalCase 'classes' and UPPER_CASE 'constants' in files that define neither, plus a `repositories.py` absent from this diff) contradict the visible code, which is consistently snake_case with typed signatures.

problems.description: New repositories.py carries a Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE violation per the SonarQube measurement (convention score 0.70). Note: most of the 16 measured violations live in files this commit never touched (celery_config.py, conftest.py, email_tasks.py), so they are pre-existing, not introduced here.

Store-wide read/write/migration I/O (read_store/write_store and the init_store seed write) is routed through UserRepository rather than a dedicated store/unit-of-work owner, so the whole-store lifecycle is owned by an entity repository.
`data_file=lambda: DATA_FILE` in app.py is a redundant indirection — DATA_FILE is already resolved at module import, so the repository instances could take the value directly.

strengths: Clean repository-layer extraction: BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository pull all storage access out of app.py, leaving routes and error handling as the only concerns there
Behavior-preserving: keeps the flat-file storage constraint, the shared threading lock, and the existing route/API surface intact
Idiomatic per-entity design with abstract entity_name/next_id_key and generic CRUD, reducing the 117 deleted lines of duplicated inline file I/O
SonarQube confirms quality: bugs +0, smells -1, duplications +0.0%
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, behavior-preserving repository refactor that improves separation of concerns and reduces code smells, with only minor convention and store-ownership nits.

problems.description: The limiter defaults to redis://localhost:6379 with no in-process/memory fallback, so the entire API fails closed (500s on every request) if Redis is unavailable — a hard runtime dependency that also contradicts the module's stated 'flat-file JSON storage, no databases' design, and it makes the test suite depend on a live Redis on 6379 (the conftest limiter.reset() swallows failures but requests then 500 instead of returning 200/429).

flask_limiter (and its limits/redis deps) are added as imports but the story repo has no requirements.txt or dependency manifest, so the new dependency is undeclared and unpinned — portability risk for a flat-file demo app.

paginate_for_owner loads, filters, and sorts the entire store in memory per request (O(n)); consistent with the pre-existing list_for_owner pattern it replaces, so not a regression, but the cursor API implies scalability it doesn't deliver.
test_rate_limit_uses_redis_storage asserts on the private _storage_uri attribute of flask_limiter's Limiter — a white-box, brittle test that will break on a library upgrade.
_rate_limit_key duplicates the JWT decode + PyJWTError handling already implemented in the auth_required decorator, so token parsing now lives in two places and can drift.

GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare JSON array to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking client contract; acceptable mid-story and the existing tests are updated, but it should be documented as a deliberate API change.

strengths: Cross-cutting scope is executed on-theme: rate limiting and cursor pagination land exactly in the 'cross_cutting' session and route through the existing repository layer (Route handlers never touch storage directly) rather than new subsystems.

Cursor-based keyset pagination is implemented correctly: limit+1 has_more detection, 100-item cap, 400 on non-integer cursor, per-owner scoping, preserved total, and unknown-cursor semantics documented in the paginate_for_owner docstring.

19 new tests plus updated existing tests cover response shape, cursor walking with no-overlap assertions, limit capping, invalid/unknown cursors, owner isolation, per-user rate limits, Retry-After header, and auth endpoints — strong coverage for both features.
Rate-limit keys are per-authenticated-user with IP fallback for /auth/* and are scoped by DATA_FILE, so tests isolate cleanly and shared-IP users aren't throttled together.

The commit's own code is convention-clean: snake_case functions, a correctly UPPER_CASE RATE_LIMIT constant, type hints and a docstring on the public signature — it introduces none of the measured violations.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped, well-tested cross-cutting session (per-user rate limiting + correct cursor pagination through the existing repository layer), rated better than the parent despite the hard Redis dependency that fails the API closed; note the discrepancy that the measured 0.70 convention score is dominated by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, email_tasks.py) and analyzer false positives (the diff adds +0 classes yet is flagged 'Classes should use PascalCase'), so the commit's own additions are convention-clean.

compounding_issues: Session 1 replaced the seed's SQLite with a JSON flat-file store + threading.Lock; every later session pays for it — pagination, owner filtering, and concurrency are hand-rolled, and the 'no databases' premise erodes once Session 3 (Celery/Redis) and Session 5 (flask-limiter Redis storage) pull in Redis anyway
The `_migrate` legacy-user block keeps being patched per feature (Session 3 had to retrofit `email` onto the legacy user), accumulating migration debt each time a user field is added
The completion-notification trigger lives inline in the `edit_task` route, so Session 4's repository refactor split persistence but not domain logic from transport
Dev default SECRET_KEY is a short 14-byte string that trips PyJWT's InsecureKeyLengthWarning, and the JWT `sub` is stored as a string forcing int() coercion at every auth read
key_decisions: Session 1: rewrote the seed from SQLite to a JSON flat-file store with a module-level threading lock — simple and dependency-free but a step back from relational storage
Session 2: added JWT (HS256) auth with owner-scoped task access plus a legacy-user migration path so pre-existing stores survive the schema change
Session 3: integrated async email notifications via Celery with a Redis broker, routed to a dedicated 'email' queue and fired on the status→completed transition
Session 4: extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository ABC with entity_name/next_id_key contract, TaskRepository/UserRepository), slimming app.py down to routes + auth

Session 5: applied cross-cutting hardening — per-user rate limiting (flask-limiter, JWT-keyed, Redis storage) and cursor-based pagination that deliberately changed the GET /tasks response shape to {data, next_cursor, total}
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically. The test suite grew 10 → 24 → 32 → 32 → 50 across sessions with every session ending green (the final tree passes all 50), and the codebase got structurally cleaner over time. Session 2 had a brief debugging dip — 13 failures from the pre-auth tests before the agent updated them — and Session 5 iterated through a few failing edge-case runs (47/49 → 50) while landing the new pagination and rate-limit tests, but neither left lasting damage. Features accumulated in a sensible order — auth before ownership-sensitive work, a repository refactor before adding cross-cutting concerns — so the Session 5 hardening slots cleanly on top of Session 4's repository API.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc — greenfield rewrite, JWT auth, Celery integration, repository refactor, cross-cutting hardening — that lands green with a 50-test suite; its only persistent blemish is the Session 1 flat-file storage choice that later sessions kept having to engineer around.
